title: The Uman Encirclement
subtitle: Breakout attempts, captivity and the closing routes of two armies
author: Robert M. Dobo
phase: II — The Drive into the Soviet Interior
summary: The encircled Soviet 6th and 12th Armies requested air support and ammunition while attempting to break out. Their final reports expose the limits of further resistance; evidence of captivity and early occupation killings follows the consequences beyond the battlefield.
body:
The message received at 03:00 on 6 August 1941 put the contradiction starkly. The Soviet 6th and 12th Armies were encircled near Podvysokoye; ammunition and fuel were gone. Yet headquarters still reported twenty thousand bayonets and proposed striking south towards Pervomaysk to join the 18th Army. It asked for air attacks, ammunition and signals for coordinating with aircraft. The plan required help from outside the pocket at the very moment when its own resources were failing. The document preserves an attempt to organise escape, not simply a declaration that resistance had ended. [1]a

The Uman battle had brought two Soviet armies into a narrowing space between German forces and obstructed routes. Fighting continued after 6 August, but their commanders could no longer choose among the movements that had been possible in July. The record follows the contraction: a lost connection with a neighbouring army, a proposed relief attack that could not arrive in time, requests for ammunition, and a warning that even a liaison officer could no longer be received safely. Defeat then placed surviving soldiers under German custody, where racial policy and deliberate deprivation created dangers distinct from those of the battlefield.

The southern advance changes direction

Army Group South, commanded by Rundstedt, had advanced more slowly than the German formations on the central axis during the invasion’s opening weeks. Soviet resistance and counterattacks imposed substantial demands, while the geography of Ukraine offered several objectives that could not all be pursued by the same force at once. Kiev, the Dnieper crossings, the Soviet armies farther west, and the communications toward the Black Sea were related but distinct problems. The German operation that developed around Uman sought to destroy Soviet forces west of the Dnieper before they could withdraw into a new defensive position. [2]

Kleist’s 1st Panzer Group supplied the mobile arm of this operation. After the July advance into the region west of Kiev, its movement turned south and southeast, threatening the rear of Soviet armies retreating from the west. Carl Heinrich von Stülpnagel’s 17th Army advanced from that western direction toward the area between Uman and Pervomaysk. The combination mattered: the mobile force could reach behind the Soviet troops, while the infantry army pressed them toward the narrowing space. Neither the direction nor the result should be confused with Guderian’s later movement south from Army Group Centre, which belongs to a subsequent stage of the campaign. [2] [3]b

Muzychenko’s 6th Army and Ponedelin’s 12th Army needed more than permission to move east. Their withdrawal required routes that would remain accessible long enough for infantry, guns, transport and wounded men to pass, together with a receiving position connected to neighbouring forces. German mobile formations sought to seize those connections while pressure from the west prevented an orderly disengagement. The time between issuing an instruction and completing the movement became decisive. A route available to headquarters when it planned the withdrawal could be lost before the last formations reached it, leaving successive parts of the army in increasingly different situations.

The 26th Army’s order of 26 July identifies an early break in the Soviet position. Fyodor Kostenko’s command described the 6th Army as its neighbour on the left and immediately acknowledged that it had no tactical contact with it. German tank and motorised infantry groups had pushed formations back, requiring defensive positions and local counterattacks. The missing connection mattered more than the apparent continuity of the army designations. Kostenko could assign a boundary, but he could not thereby guarantee that troops on the other side were still available to protect it. [4]c

A transfer of command during retreat

On 25 July, Budenny’s Southwestern Direction headquarters transferred the 6th and 12th Armies to Southern Front, effective at 20:00. The receiving command was to begin withdrawing them after dark towards the Zvenigorodka–Talnoye–Khristinovka line and establish a defence. The order recognized the danger and authorized withdrawal before the final pocket formed. Its execution depended on finding routes the armies could still reach.[5]

The transfer placed the armies under Tyulenev’s Southern Front while Budenny retained responsibility for the wider southwestern direction. To become effective, the new relationship required reliable information about locations, strength, existing instructions and supply arrangements. The directive’s demands for acknowledgement, reports on orders issued and confirmation of handover addressed those requirements. Administrative procedure was therefore part of restoring operational control during retreat. The transfer offered a basis for coordination with forces to the south, but its value depended on completing that work while the German advance was altering the situation the receiving headquarters had to understand. [5]d

To the south, the 18th Army confronted the same developing danger from another direction. At 14:00 on 31 July, its commander, Andrei Smirnov, reported measures against the German grouping near Golovanevsk. He asked that Muzychenko attack toward a line including Ladyzhinka and neighbouring settlements, while requesting at least a division from the front reserve to cover the Sinyukha River and secure the rear of three armies. The report warned that without this stabilisation their combined actions would not overcome the enemy penetration. It was an appeal for coordinated action and a defensive safeguard, rather than evidence that either had already been achieved. [6]

Smirnov proposed using the 169th Rifle Division against the Golovanevsk threat while other troops held the army’s position. His request reveals the competing functions imposed on limited forces. The same army needed to attack northward, retain its own front, and avoid being cut off from the east. A relief operation could not be detached from those requirements. If the 18th Army itself withdrew south, the distance separating it from the threatened armies would increase. By early August, that was precisely the problem the higher command was forced to acknowledge. [6]e

The routes close around the armies

The 26th Army’s defensive arrangements show how commanders tried to deal with penetration when continuous contact had been lost. Its 116th Rifle Division was ordered to send two battalion-sized blocking detachments by truck, provided with antitank artillery, toward threatened roads farther south. Another division was to protect its southern flank with a blocking force near Lisyanka and reconnoitre toward Zvenigorodka. These were attempts to restore information and place obstacles on routes the enemy might exploit. They did not amount to a restored link with the 6th Army. Moving a battalion quickly could cover a road temporarily, but holding a broader interval required infantry, artillery, communications, and reserves that the command still had to assemble. [4]

Rifle troops were to relieve cavalry on the night of 26–27 July, releasing the cavalry for army reserve. The order’s blocking detachments had tactical tasks against German penetration: road protection, reconnaissance and antitank defence. The term does not establish that these were punitive detachments shooting Soviet stragglers. Kostenko was securing exposed routes while trying to recover a reserve.[4]f

Uman lay north of the final concentration of trapped troops. The battle’s name should not obscure its shifting geography: Podvysokoye and the wooded area known as Zelenaya Brama became central to the last Soviet resistance, while Pervomaysk lay farther south at an important river junction. The Sinyukha, flowing toward the Southern Bug, formed an obstacle on the eastern side of the threatened area. Rivers that might have supported a new defensive position became barriers to escape when their crossings were held or covered by German forces. A retreating column needed a route for guns and vehicles as well as a passage for individual soldiers. [1] [2]

Accounts assign different dates to the closing of the encirclement, partly because initial contacts, the consolidation of the ring, and the ending of organised resistance were separate events. The German Historical Museum’s account places the junction southeast of Uman on 3 August and dates the principal fighting through 8 August. The contemporary Soviet report of 4 August confirms that the German force coming through Zvenigorodka had joined troops advancing from the west. These records support an encirclement consolidated in the opening days of August, while providing no justification for treating every possible exit as sealed at one precisely established hour. [7] [8]

Budenny’s report to Stalin on 4 August described the broader consequences with unusual clarity. The 18th Army was withdrawing south and sharply widening the gap separating it from the encircled armies. German forces threatened Southern Front’s right flank and rear across a broad stretch from Kirovograd to Pervomaysk. Mobile reserves were needed, but none were available; newly forming divisions were unready and far from the decisive area. Thus the defeat was not confined to the shrinking pocket. Its development was forcing the command to reconsider the survival and movement of the rest of Southern Front. [8]

The same report identified limits to the proposed Soviet response. Counterattacks from the Kiev and Kanev areas could not be synchronised before approximately 10–12 August because forces were still concentrating. Budenny sought to accelerate the Kanev effort to 6–7 August, but doubted that the newly assembled divisions could do more than temporarily divert German attention. Their combat cohesion was inadequate, and the enemy was strengthening in the sector. This was a candid distinction between a desirable operational result and the smaller effect the available force might produce. The trapped armies, meanwhile, could not wait indefinitely for the concentration to finish. [8]g

The shrinking resources of 6 August

The estimate of twenty thousand bayonets at 03:00 concerned infantry fighting strength. Staff, artillerymen, transport personnel and wounded soldiers could remain outside that category. The force available for a breakout was therefore smaller than the population whose escape depended on it. It cannot be compared directly with prisoner returns covering a wider operation and a later interval.[1]

The proposed movement south also required a rearguard facing north. Even at this late stage, the command was attempting to organise a military withdrawal, with part of the force covering the movement of the rest. That arrangement created a terrible practical difficulty. Troops assigned to hold back the enemy needed ammunition and a later opportunity to disengage; the main force needed enough strength to break through another part of the ring. The report’s inventory of shortages indicates how little freedom remained to satisfy both demands. The plan depended on external assistance that the army urgently requested but could not itself provide.

Ponedelin’s brief report on the night attack stated that it had failed and that fighting continued. He asked for bombing at Ternovka. Another message, from military council member Kulikov, requested urgent attacks at Ternovka and Pokotilovo; it was marked as received at 13:25 on 6 August. A later endorsement stated that available aviation had been directed there. The endorsement records a command response, but it does not by itself establish the number of aircraft arriving, the bombs delivered, or the effect on the ground. These distinctions are essential when reconstructing whether a trapped force actually received the support its messages requested. [9] [10]

The requests continued into plans for the following night. The 12th Army staff asked for systematic bombing around a list of settlements on the encirclement perimeter during 6 August and the night of 6–7 August. Southern Front staff identified the message as a radio interception and instructed its aviation command to organise night attacks. The survival of this exchange shows that information could still pass out of the pocket, but through imperfect channels. It also establishes that fighting was expected to continue beyond the study’s anchor date. A narrative that ends the battle on 6 August would contradict the defenders’ own dated operational messages. [11]h

The space needed for liaison

No safe place for a messenger

A message marked received at 14:20 on 6 August reported that Ponedelin could not accept a liaison delegate. He believed there was no safe landing area and that a parachutist would be shot. The telegram records his assessment, not an attempted descent. The defended space had contracted so far that sending someone to restore contact itself seemed impracticable.[12]i

Air support and the evacuation problem

The army’s requests for ammunition by air illustrate the final contraction of its supply system. Ordinary deliveries required roads, crossings, and receiving points that were no longer secure. Aircraft offered a possible alternative, but the receiving troops needed to identify themselves and recover loads under fire. The 03:00 message specifically asked for coordination signals, showing that this procedure could not be assumed. Delivering ammunition was a separate task from bombing the enemy, and neither could be inferred simply from the existence of Soviet aircraft elsewhere in the theatre. [1]

Budenny had already warned on 4 August that aviation was the principal force still contesting the German outflanking movement, but that it was insufficient. Three reinforcing air regiments had not arrived, and rainy weather since 1 August had sharply restricted operations. This places a documented weather limitation at a specific point in the battle. It also exposes the difference between reinforcement allocated and reinforcement available. An army awaiting support gained nothing immediately from an air regiment still en route, and a regiment that arrived could still face weather and basing constraints. [8]j

The wounded needed routes that attendants and transport could use. Fuel shortages and contracting defended space reduced their chances of evacuation even where fit men might escape in small groups. The messages give no dependable total of the wounded remaining, but establish constraints that affected them with particular severity.

The failed night attack and renewed calls for air support show the command continuing to seek escape. Individual groups could still resist as ammunition dwindled and the armies lost the means to act together. Their subsequent mass capture does not prove a collective decision to abandon the war without fighting.

Prisoners and the uses of defeat

The principal battle continued through 8 August in the German Historical Museum’s chronology. More than one hundred thousand Soviet prisoners is the broad figure given in both its account and the U.S. Army synthesis. That figure describes the outcome of the larger operation, not a verified count of captives already assembled on 6 August. Nor should it be treated as a total of soldiers killed. Captured men, dead men, wounded men, and troops who escaped belong to different categories, even when wartime reporting blurred their boundaries. [7] [2]

The United States Holocaust Memorial Museum’s photograph dated 14 August shows a German soldier guarding Soviet prisoners at Uman after the main battle. It supplies no count of the camp’s population or deaths. It records survivors passing into a system in which German authorities controlled food, shelter, labour and treatment. Those decisions created further dangers after the fighting ended.[13]k

German treatment of Soviet prisoners was shaped by racial and political policy. Grossly inadequate food and shelter exposed men weakened by battle to further deprivation. A supply system strained by the advance did not make prisoners’ survival an impossibility beyond human choice: the authorities decided what provision and protection they would receive. The mass mortality that followed must retain its actual chronology rather than being compressed into the Uman battle. The distinction establishes the captors’ responsibility without assigning later deaths to an unsupported local count. [14]l

Moskalchuk and Chornyi distinguish photographs taken in different circumstances and reject treating a posed image as proof of voluntary betrayal. Ponedelin and Kirillov were executed after their return to Soviet custody, on 25 August 1950, and rehabilitated on 29 February 1956. Their later punishment does not establish an intention in August 1941. The battle’s own messages instead record requests for aid and attempted breakouts.[15]m

Civilians in the battlefield and the occupied town

The military collapse also changed the position of Uman’s inhabitants and those living along the armies’ routes. The closing of a road affected refugees as well as soldiers; the presence of troops increased demands for transport, food, and shelter; and the movement of the front exposed residents to new authorities. These consequences were not experienced uniformly. Jewish residents faced persecution directed at their identity, while other civilians encountered occupation through requisition, labour demands, violence, and the destruction or interruption of ordinary livelihoods. An army-level account must leave room for these different experiences without assigning a single response to an entire population.

Evidence associated with postwar proceedings against Günther Herrmann, the former commander of Sonderkommando 4b of Einsatzgruppe C, places the murder of approximately one hundred Jews at a gravel pit in or near Uman in early August 1941. The Yad Vashem account, reproduced in dekoder’s historical mapping project, does not provide a precise day. It supports the presence of organised anti-Jewish killing at the beginning of occupation, without requiring the atlas to date it specifically to 6 August. The perpetrators and the evidentiary basis can be identified even where the chronology remains approximate. [16]n

Buzia Leibovych’s later escape

After her parents and sister were killed, Buzia Leibovych survived imprisonment in several labour camps before escaping. The National Museum of the History of Ukraine in the Second World War recounts her appeal to the Boius family at Rosishky. They hid her until liberation in March 1944. This was a later struggle under occupation, separate from the encirclement on 6 August, and depended on finding people prepared to shelter her.[17]o

What the victory opened, and what it left unresolved

The Uman defeat widened German opportunities toward the lower Dnieper and the Black Sea. It also forced Soviet leaders to distinguish between positions they hoped to retain and forces they could still save. Budenny’s report of 4 August proposed withdrawing Southern Front toward the Ingul and Nikolaev while assigning Odessa’s defence to the Separate Coastal Army. He requested that the Black Sea Fleet organise and protect maritime communications. The proposal linked a land withdrawal to continued resistance at a port supplied by sea, anticipating a different operational problem from the one that had destroyed the armies near Uman. [8]

The same report described long stretches of the Dnieper as inadequately covered and proposed moving newly forming divisions before their preparation was complete. It named formations for sectors around Kremenchug, Dnepropetrovsk, Zaporozhye, and Nikopol, while acknowledging that some had no established readiness date. This was the wider cost of the defeat. The Soviet command had to rebuild a front with formations whose limitations were known, because waiting for complete preparation risked leaving essential crossings unprotected. German success created new objectives; Soviet survival depended on assembling another defence quickly enough to contest them. [8]p

Hopkins’s discussions with Stalin on 31 July help mark the distance between a prospective coalition war and the battle ending at Uman. Their conversation concerned equipment and transport routes whose military value would emerge over time. The men attempting to break out needed ammunition that night. No future supply programme could answer that request. The defeat therefore belongs within the wider transition to a longer war while retaining its own finality for the formations destroyed and the people killed, captured or left behind. [18]q

Defeat at Uman opened another stage of danger for prisoners and occupied communities while German operations continued towards the lower Dnieper. The war was also widening elsewhere. The next study follows the defence of Odessa and the Soviet counterstroke near Staraya Russa alongside the violence behind the advance.

sourceMethod: Lettered evidence notes retain detailed references and qualifications; numbered citations lead to the sources below. Published Soviet transcriptions distinguish orders from reported results; archival locators do not imply direct inspection of original files. Where only an abstract, extract or reproduced text was available, that limit remains stated in the notes. The dated map has separate feature sources and precision notes.
